language.script_notes: Street corners commonly carry a blue enamel plate reading 'Rue de/du ...'. Departmental roads are signed 'D' + number in yellow. Bilingual French/Breton signage in Brittany, French/Corsican in Corsica (sometimes the French half is defaced), Occitan text appears in the south.

road_furniture.bollard_color: Thick white cylindrical posts with a red reflective band wrapped fully around the top — France wraps the red 100% around the cap, unlike Hungary's smaller discrete red reflector. A rarer grey-reflector variant also exists.
road_furniture.bollard_shape: Distinctive rounded post shape unlike most other European bollards; a less common wedge-shaped bollard with rectangular white reflectors front and back also appears.
road_furniture.line_paint: Center line often made of two small squares joined together ('tiret double') rather than one continuous dash — close to unique to France in Europe. Long white dashes run along both road edges, longer than almost anywhere else in Europe.
road_furniture.curb_style: Painted kerbs in towns; unremarkable elsewhere.
road_furniture.km_marker_style: Concrete square or segmented utility poles, frequently carrying a small blue rectangular plate — a near-definitive France tell. Yellow 'D' road markers for departmental routes; red-bordered white speed-limit signs; the blue 'turn right ahead' sign is square in France (round elsewhere in Europe).

architecture.roof_style: Steep dark slate roofs across the north and center (Brittany, Normandy, Corrèze); rounded overlapping clay tiles of varying colour in the south; mansard (double-pitch) roofs with dormer windows common in and around Paris.
architecture.roof_material: Slate in the north; terracotta barrel tiles in the south; fish-scale tiles and steep half-hipped roofs in Alsace.
architecture.wall_construction: Whitewashed single-story homes on the west coast; thin flat pale stone walls in the southeast (Luberon/Provence); half-timbering in Alsace (Germanic influence); dark red brick rowhouses near the Belgian border, bricks often outlined in white mortar.
architecture.wall_color_palette: Cream/pale stone through most of the country, whitewash on the Atlantic coast, warm orange/ochre render around Toulouse, dark brick in the north near Belgium, half-timber browns in Alsace.
architecture.distinctive_building_types: Mansard-roofed Parisian apartment blocks with wrought-iron balconies; half-timbered Alsatian houses; Provençal stone farmhouses (mas); bright orange-brick Toulouse townhouses with wooden shutters; village churches with a single spire.

nature.vegetation: Hedgerows, green meadows and apple orchards in Normandy; pine and spruce in the Alps and the Vosges/Jura; olive trees, vineyards and warm Mediterranean scrub in Provence and along the south coast; vineyards widespread in the southwest and Burgundy.
nature.terrain: Mostly low plains and plateaus in the north and center; the Alps (Mont Blanc, 4,808 m) and Pyrenees rising sharply in the south and southwest; rugged limestone Calanques coves along the Mediterranean coast; mountainous, Mediterranean-feeling Corsica offshore.
nature.climate_signature: Oceanic and often overcast in the northwest; continental in the east; hot and sun-bleached Mediterranean in the south — imagery ranges from grey Norman hedgerow lanes to bright Provençal stone villages.

vehicles.plate_color: White plate with a blue strip on the left (France's 'F' + EU star); a second blue strip on the right shows a regional emblem above the two-digit department number, plus an optional circular department sticker below it. Occasional fully yellow plates on older/agricultural vehicles.
vehicles.plate_format: AA-NNN-AA (two letters, three digits, two letters).
vehicles.distinctive_vehicles: Renault Twingo/Clio/Megane/Espace, Peugeot 205/208/308, Citroën with its double-chevron badge (2CV still occasionally seen). Overall a French-brand-dominated fleet, unlike Germany's or Italy's.

google_coverage.camera_generation: Mostly Gen 3 with some Gen 4 in cities; a small amount of Gen 1 exists but is far more likely encountered in the US, Australia or New Zealand.
google_coverage.coverage_notes: Dense, near-complete coverage across the whole country including rural D-roads — one of the best-covered countries in Europe.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Latin script, similar road signage style, brick rowhouses near the shared border
confusion_set.tiebreaker: France has slate roofs (north) and the white/red-band bollard with a blue utility-pole plate; Belgium leans more heavily brick and lacks France's bollard style and square keep-right sign.

confusion_set.shared_traits: French-speaking cantons, similar mountain architecture near the shared border, similar terrain in the Alps/Jura
confusion_set.tiebreaker: French plates carry the blue EU strip and department number; Swiss plates are white with a black canton code and no blue EU strip. Switzerland is generally tidier and better-maintained.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Blue-and-white chevron road-curve signs (unique to just these two countries in Europe), Mediterranean vegetation in the south
confusion_set.tiebreaker: France's square blue keep-right sign and red-banded white bollards are absent in Spain; Spanish plates are yellow-only on the rear, white in front, with no blue strip.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Mediterranean coastline and vegetation, similar terracotta roof tiles in the south
confusion_set.tiebreaker: France's blue utility-pole plates and red-topped bollards are absent in Italy; Italian plates are plain white with a blue EU strip but no department emblem.

confusion_set.shared_traits: Half-timbered architecture near Alsace, similar signage conventions
confusion_set.tiebreaker: French plates have the blue department strip vs. Germany's white plate with a city-code prefix; German town names often end in '-heim'/'-burg', which doesn't occur in France.
